task: Crossing a plateau: reaching a cheaper scheme through maps that cost the same, where a strictly descending walk cannot take a first step at all.
source: Produced by `reproduce/measure.py`, which runs `minimise-rank --plateau` and `walk-scheme` at exactly the flags each row records.
why: Steps 2 and 3 adopt a candidate only when it makes the map strictly cheaper, and on matrix multiplication no single rank-one map ever does: the shortlist for <2,2,2> is 0 of 225. Yet <2,2,2> has a 7-product algorithm. Strassen's seven are reachable from the naive eight only through maps costing the same, so a method that refuses a sideways step cannot get there by construction. These rows are what it costs to allow one.
machine: Single core of a 12th Gen Intel i5-12450H at 2.2 GHz.
readings: Two different tools cross this plateau, and a timing from one was printed beside a claim about the other. `oracle_guided_search/measurements/three-by-three.md` says `minimise_rank` cannot take a first step on <2,2,2> but `plateau_search` can, and then gives 0.11 s. That 0.11 s is `walk-scheme`'s, the figure `famous_tensors/README.md` publishes in a column it correctly labels as walk-scheme. `plateau_search` does cross, and it is not what was timed there.

What `plateau_search` costs, measured: at a 380-state budget it reaches 7 in 0.065 s having visited 386 subspaces. At the default budget of 200 000 it reaches the same 7 and takes 20 s over 66 063 subspaces, because it keeps walking after it has already seen the best map it will find.

380 is where it crosses. At 370 the walk visits 376 subspaces, takes one improvement and stays at the naive 8; at 380 it takes two, visits 386 and reaches 7. Both rows are published so the boundary itself is checked: a change that makes the crossing cheaper moves it, and a single positive row would hide that.

So `plateau_state_budget = 200 000` is 526 times what the one crossing anyone here has measured needs. `tunables.conf` marks it PROVISIONAL and never measured; it is measured now, and the default is not what that crossing wants.

The walk rows pin the three counts `famous_tensors/README.md` quotes: 7 on <2,2,2>, 9 on GF(16), and 24 on <3,3,3> from the naive 27, each over 8 independent seeds of 20 000 flips. <3,3,3> is the one shape in this repository where nothing else improves on naive at all.
limits: A plateau crossing guarantees nothing about optimality. It returns the cheapest map it ever saw, so it can only match or beat the strict walk it extends, and neither is a proof of anything. The refutations live in `exhaustive_search` and `satisfiability`.
<2,2,3> does not cross at a 2 000-state budget: the pool is 945, the shortlist is 0, and the walk stays at the naive 12. What budget it would need is not measured, so no row claims one.

The three timings quoted in prose around this file predate it and are slower than what the code now does: 0.11 s, 0.69 s and 38.1 s against 0.026 s, 0.20 s and 11.7 s today. They are not corrected here. MEASURING.md says a protocol timing is superseded by another protocol timing, and this machine was running other work; the counts are what `--check` compares and the counts are unchanged.

walk.name: GF(16) from naive, 20 000 flips over 8 seeds

counts_provenance.covers: The counts in this file and the invocations that produced them, and nothing else. Every `seconds` field here is older than this block and was not touched: a count is exact arithmetic and comes out the same on any machine, a timing does not, so `--counts` refreshes the first and leaves the second exactly as measured. What produced the timings is the `provenance` block.
counts_provenance.protocol: counts only: exact arithmetic, one run each, the machine irrelevant.
